idiom_name: switch on the discriminant with an assertNever / never assignment arm
implementation_notes: TypeScript has no match expression, so the local idiom replaces the classic structure: declare the closed set as a discriminated union with a literal tag, switch on the discriminant so each arm narrows to exactly one member, and let the default arm assign the residual subject to never - or pass it to an assertNever(x: never): never helper - which turns a missing arm into a compile error. Keep strictNullChecks on, because the never argument depends on sound narrowing, and declare closed sets as type aliases rather than interfaces, since interfaces merge by declaration and a union of interfaces can silently grow elsewhere in the program.
pitfalls: Without strictNullChecks - or with an any/unknown escape in the union - the residual type may not narrow to never, and the arm silently stops checking anything.
Declaration merging grows interfaces: a union of interfaces can gain members elsewhere and the exhaustiveness error disappears; use type aliases for closed sets.
A switch statement without a never default is perfectly legal and simply does nothing for an unhandled variant, so the check exists only where that arm is written.

variants.name: ts-pattern match().with(...).exhaustive()
variants.implementation_notes: ts-pattern implements the match expression in userland: match(subject).with(pattern, handler) chains with P.select, P.union, P.when and nested object/array/tuple patterns, closed by .exhaustive(), which proves coverage through the type system (an unhandled member surfaces as NonExhaustiveError<T>) and throws at run time if a value arrives that the types did not predict. Reach for it when patterns are nested or when matching happens on values that are not already narrowed unions, since the switch/never idiom makes you write that narrowing by hand. Version 5 requires TypeScript 5 or newer because it relies on const type parameters.
variants.code_sketch:
import { match } from 'ts-pattern';

const area = (s: Shape) =>
  match(s)
    .with({ kind: 'circle' }, ({ r }) => Math.PI * r ** 2)
    .with({ kind: 'rect' }, ({ w, h }) => w * h)
    .exhaustive();   // NonExhaustiveError<...> if a variant is missing
pitfalls: Coverage can only be proved for a closed union: matching a widened type (string, any) falls back to .otherwise() and the guarantee is gone.
Using .otherwise() instead of .exhaustive() is legal and drops the compile-time check silently, so keep the exhaustive call in review guidelines.
Handlers are evaluated eagerly since v5 and every .with() is runtime work, so a long chain in a hot path costs more than a compiled switch.
